questions.q: When would you reach for the HTTP action instead of a pre-built connector?
options: Whenever calling any Microsoft service, even if a connector exists
When calling an endpoint that has no pre-built Power Automate connector, such as a custom internal API
Only when the flow has no trigger
HTTP actions and connectors can never be used in the same flow
questions.explain: The HTTP action is the general-purpose fallback for calling any URL, used specifically when no pre-built connector exists for that service.

questions.q: Which five fields does every HTTP action let you configure?
options: Trigger, Action, Condition, Loop, Variable
Method, URI, Headers, Queries, Body
Name, Type, Value, Format, Schema
Connector, Auth, Scope, Retry, Timeout
questions.explain: An HTTP action configures Method, URI, Headers, Queries, and Body — the same fields any general-purpose HTTP client needs.

questions.q: Where would you typically put an API key to authenticate an HTTP action's call to a third-party service?
options: In the Method field
In a Headers field, such as Authorization or x-api-key
It's impossible to authenticate an HTTP action
Only in the Queries field, never Headers
questions.explain: An API key or bearer token is most commonly sent as a header, such as Authorization: Bearer <key>, depending on what the target API expects.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about hardcoding a raw API key directly into a flow's Headers field?
options: It's the recommended approach for all cases
It's a bad habit to avoid; production should use something like Azure Key Vault instead
Power Automate blocks this from happening automatically
It's required because connection references don't support API keys
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out hardcoding keys as a bad habit, recommending a production-safe pattern like Key Vault instead, covered in a later chapter.

questions.q: What three things does an HTTP action's output include for use in later steps?
options: Headers, body, and status code
Only the status code
A screenshot of the response
The original request URI only
questions.explain: An HTTP action's output includes headers, body, and status code — the body usually holds the data you want, and the status code is used to branch on success or failure.
